transcript: Does anyone else feel like theater artists undervalue the importance of actors being able to comfortably do an accent or a dialect? When I used to do theater, I feel like the sentiment from writers and directors was always like, the accent will come later. And I'm like, yeah, but, like, will it? Actually, it's always, the acting should come first, which I agree with in theory. The problem is that a bad accent, I think, can actually make the acting worse because the actor isn't comfortable. Like, you can sense even from the audience that the accent is an obstacle for them. And I've seen this even at the highest level of theater, and there are ways around it that are being underutilized. Like, the most recent Broadway revival of the Crucible was LED by British actors Ben Wishaw and Sophie Okenedo, and they did the first couple previews using American dialects, but then they switched to their native dialects because it just wasn't clicking. And I actually saw the production both ways, and their performances or so much better using their native dialects. And yeah, I think the industry could be prioritizing accent work in the casting process a little more than they currently are, either by hiring actors who natively have the dialect you need or actors who are just already very comfortable putting it on. But the really underrated move is doing what they did in the crucible. Just don't do the dialect. We see this With Shakespeare all the time. Like, you never see an American production of Richard the third where they're doing English accents, but they say they're in England, and we believe them. And, yes, it's easier to get away with in Shakespeare for a variety of reasons, but I. I still think we can start applying the same principle to more shows than we currently are, especially when it's a period piece, when it's not as rooted in realism, when all of the characters have the same dialect as each other. So you can kind of broadly apply this internally consistent suspension of disbelief. In taking this idea even further, we could even have a process for playwright approved localization of scripts. But maybe that's a conversation for a different video. And of course, this doesn't apply to everything. Sometimes the material really does demand realistic, location specific dialects for the characters, but you'd be surprised how many times that's not the case, and they still have the actors do the dialect anyway, and then it's bad. And even when the material really does call for a dialect, you could still ask the question, would you rather have the audience be distracted by the lack of a dialect or a badly executed dialect? Personally, I find a badly executed dialect a lot more distracting, especially, like I said earlier, if it appears to be getting in the actor's way. But I know this is gonna vary from audience member to audience. Member so? I'm curious to hear what you guys think.
